claims.statement: Dnyaneshwar / Jnanadeva is a medieval Marathi poet-philosopher associated with Nath and Varkari traditions.
The reference entry gives birth alternatives 1271 or 1275, and 1296 as the traditional departure year.
claims.caution: Do not convert a conventional lifespan into an independently proved exact birth date.

claims.statement: Dnyaneshwari, Amritanubhava and Changdev Pasashti form the central philosophical corpus.
The large attributed abhanga corpus contains material whose authorship is questioned.
claims.caution: Do not authenticate a verse solely from a signature or website title.

claims.statement: Works such as Uttaragita, Prakritagita, Panchikarana and Shukashtaka require separate attribution review.
claims.caution: Not incorporated as securely authored primary works.

claims.statement: Dnyaneshwari explicitly presents itself as a Marathi exposition of the Krishna–Arjuna discourse in the Mahabharata.
The received closing verse gives Shaka 1212; the authenticity of this dating verse has been questioned.
claims.caution: Conventional 1290 date and textual-critical qualification are both retained.

claims.statement: Eknath is associated with recension and correction of the received Dnyaneshwari.
claims.caution: Later colophon verses are not automatically Dnyaneshwar’s own words.

claims.statement: The consulted Wikisource chapter 7 repeats chapter 6.
claims.caution: Alternate chapter 7 is a separate witness, not a silent critical repair.

claims.statement: This Haripath source numbers 29 entries, while entry 28 mentions twenty-eight abhangas.
claims.caution: Do not erase the additional entry or equate count with authorship.

claims.statement: The imported Changdev Pasashti witness has 65 numbered verses.
Pasaydan belongs to the closing section of Dnyaneshwari rather than being a separate original treatise.
The opening uses the Vedas, Smriti, eighteen Puranas, six philosophies and ten Upanishads in its literary imagery.
claims.caution: A category reference does not demonstrate consultation of every member text.

claims.statement: The received conclusion names a Nath guru lineage leading to Nivruttinath and Jnanadeva.
claims.caution: Lineage narrative and historical dating of each link are distinct questions.

claims.statement: Nivruttinath is represented as both elder brother and guru in the tradition.
Vitthalpant, Rukmini, Nivruttinath, Sopan and Muktabai belong to the received family biography.
claims.caution: Specific incidents depend on later narratives.

claims.statement: Namdev Gatha saint-life sections have transmission and namesake problems.
claims.caution: Do not assume every biographical section was composed by the contemporary Namdev.

claims.statement: Buffalo recitation and the moving wall belong to devotional saint-life narration.
claims.caution: Presented as traditions, not independently verified physical events.

claims.statement: Alandi’s samadhi shrine is an important object of devotional practice and scholarly study.
claims.caution: Shrine history does not independently establish every detail of the saint’s final event.

claims.statement: Vernacular accessibility and social inequality must be studied together in Jnanesvari.
claims.caution: A modern interpretation should be attributed to its scholar.

claims.statement: The received text opens with Shiva–Shakti imagery and develops reflection on experience, knowledge and nonduality.
Comparisons with Vedanta, Nath yoga and Shaiva thought require argument, not automatic identity.
claims.caution: Similar vocabulary is not sufficient evidence of direct textual borrowing.

claims.statement: Vedic Samhitas, Brahmanas, Aranyakas and Upanishads are distinguished from later philosophical and devotional literature.
claims.caution: Gita, Puranas and Yoga Sutra should not all be labelled Vedas.

claims.statement: This database is not a complete corpus of every Vedic and ancient Indian text.
claims.caution: The classical inventory identifies coverage and untested comparisons explicitly.
